newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian net exports set to boost GDP in Q3.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian net exports set to boost GDP in Q3.

text.p: Another upbeat performance on the trade front should keep Australia's current account deficit at tolerable levels in September and ensure that net exports make a heathly contribution to economic growth in the quarter.

The data, out Wednesday, are expected to show a shortfall of A$1.3 billion against A$1.33 billion in August. This would be the fourth sub-A$1.5 billion result in a row and compares with average monthly deficits in 1995/96 of A$1.66 billion.
Analysts said such a steady outcome would reassure investors the deficit was not a brake on growth, but was unlikely to have a great impact given their preoccupation with monetary policy.
The data would, however, provide another piece of the jigsaw for estimating gross domestic product for the September quarter and all the signs favoured a solid boost to growth.
"Our forecasts see a one percent rise in export volumes and a two percent fall in imports volumes for the quarter," said Andrew Ticehurst, an analyst at Macquarie Bank.
"That implies a 0.6 percentage point contribution to third quarter expenditure-based GDP from the trade in goods and services," Ticehurst said.
This would mark a sharp turnaround from the second quarter when net exports detracted 0.9 point from GDP growth.
David Bassanese, senior economist at Bankers Trust, was even "As a preliminary forecast, net exports will contribute around one percentage point to growth in the September quarter," he said.
For the September current account, imports had already been reported as rising 0.45 percent, while most analysts looked for exports to be broadly flat following August's 2.5 percent rise.
"In original terms, both cereal and meat exports are expected to be higher, though a stronger A$ in the month will have a dampening effect on overall export prices," Bassanese said.

The surplus on net services, such as banking and education, was tipped to bounce after a flat result in August, so analysts expected the overall goods and services account to remain in surplus for the fourth consecutive month.

The net income deficit, which measures such cross border flows as interest payments on the country's massive foreign debt, would again overshadow the improved trade performance but at least was not expected to worsen from the A$1.64 billion reported in August.
The income deficit has averaged A$1.66 billion for the last six months leaving the balance on trade as the main swing factor in the current account.
Since imports are known and a sharp fall in exports was not expected, economists' forecasts for the deficit are clustered in a relatively narrow range of A$1.2 billion to A$1.4 billion.
Anything within that would cause few ripples in the markets.
Bassanese cautioned that this might, however, be the last month of such benign current account deficits.
"Next quarter the net income deficit will be higher, due to dividend payments abroad, and imports should begin to pick up on the back of higher investment," he said.
